EMR: oxygen, BVM, naloxone (intranasal or auto-injector), unit-dose hazmat antidote auto-injectors, tourniquet, wound packing, emergency moves, manual stabilization; no pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring or transport. EMT adds pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, oral glucose, aspirin, the patient's own nitroglycerin, an inhaled bronchodilator, CPAP, the epinephrine auto-injector. AEMT adds IV and IO access, non-medicated IV fluids, supraglottic airways, waveform capnography, sublingual nitroglycerin and a limited list of IV and IM drugs (dextrose, naloxone). Paramedic adds 12-lead interpretation, manual defibrillation, synchronized cardioversion, transcutaneous pacing, needle chest decompression, intubation and medicated infusions. No newer model was found on 2026-11-17.

brief.situation: 23:50. You are a paramedic with an EMT partner; police have secured the scene. Darius, 24, was stabbed once in the left chest. He was talking when the police arrived; he lost consciousness as you pulled up. Now he has no pulse.
handover: You carry a monitor-defibrillator, BVM and airways, decompression needles, chest seals, IV and IO supplies and normal saline. Epinephrine is in the drug box.
A Level I trauma center is 12 minutes away.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated seconds per real second. Pause any time.
Every assessment and treatment takes the time it would on a real call. Scene time and the drive run on the clock.
Partway through you are asked to explain your decisions in writing. The case ends when care is handed over, then a debrief scores what you did.

safetyNote: Teaching case for exam practice; fictional patient. Not medical advice; follow your local protocols and medical direction.

why.question: Why did you treat this differently from a medical cardiac arrest?

parts.label: Reversible causes
parts.criteria: Traumatic arrest from a chest stab: treat the reversible causes first: bilateral needle decompression for tension pneumothorax (absent left breath sounds, full neck veins), hemorrhage control, ventilation, volume; CPR benefit is limited and should not delay these.
parts.modelAnswer: A stab to the left chest with no breath sounds and full neck veins: tension pneumothorax until proven otherwise. Bilateral decompression came before compressions or drugs.

parts.label: Time and place
parts.criteria: Minimal scene time; CPR, if any, en route; a Level I trauma center with notification; epinephrine is not the priority in traumatic arrest.
parts.modelAnswer: On scene only for the decompressions, out within minutes to the trauma center, notified on the way; drugs were not the answer.

expertPath.text: No pulse, stab to the left chest, no left breath sounds, full neck veins: traumatic arrest, likely tension pneumothorax.
BVM; left then right needle decompression: pulse back. Vented seal.
Scoop and go to the Level I center; IO and fluid en route; notify.

rosc.headline: Treat the cause, then go
rosc.body: In traumatic arrest the reversible causes come first. Bilateral decompression gave him his pulse back, and a short scene got him to surgeons.

arrived.headline: Pulse back, by a slower route
arrived.body: Look at the scene time, both sides decompressed, and whether drugs took the place of the cause.

noRosc.headline: The cause was in his chest
noRosc.body: Compressions and epinephrine do not fix a tension pneumothorax. Decompress both sides first.

scoring.modelReasoning: Traumatic cardiac arrest from a left chest stab: treat the reversible causes first (NASEMSO). Absent left breath sounds and full neck veins point to tension pneumothorax: bilateral needle decompression at once, ventilation, a vented seal, hemorrhage control and volume en route. CPR has limited benefit and, if done, happens en route; epinephrine is not the priority. Keep the scene short and take him to the Level I trauma center with notification.

first.ask: As the needle goes in: what comes first in a traumatic arrest like this one?

choices.label: Treating the reversible cause: decompress both sides
Twenty minutes of CPR on scene

first.explain: NASEMSO: in traumatic arrest, perform bilateral rapid chest decompression and manage hemorrhage; evidence for CPR is limited, and if done it should be en route.
